summary: Eastvale's median household income of $161,322 ranks among the highest of any city its size in the Inland Empire — yet the home price-to-income ratio sits around 4.7x, substantially more manageable than coastal Southern California cities where that figure regularly clears 8x or 9x. That's the central riddle of this place: a 70,000-person city that incorporated only in 2010, carved from unincorporated Riverside County dairy land that has been almost entirely replaced by master-planned subdivisions in under two decades. The terrain is dead flat, sitting on the Santa Ana River floodplain with open-sky views east toward the distant San Bernardino Mountains, and summers push daily highs well into the 90s with nearly ten hours of sunshine — air conditioning isn't optional. Eastvale functions overwhelmingly as a bedroom community; the Ontario/Jurupa Valley logistics corridor and its massive warehouse economy sits adjacent, but many wage-earners commute west on the 60 or 91 toward Orange and Los Angeles counties, routes notorious for grinding congestion. With a 3.6% poverty rate and a violent crime rate of roughly 134 per 100,000 — low by regional standards — the infrastructure is new but the commercial fabric is still catching up, heavy on big-box retail and chain dining rather than a distinct walkable core. Eastvale is essentially a case study in whether a brand-new city can build an identity faster than its subdivisions fill up.
